pages.text:
3. A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Crossover
Trial of Intravenous Immunoglobin in the Treatment
of Anti-GAD Antibody–Positive Patients With
Stiff-Person Syndrome
Marinos C. Dalakas, Mavis Fujii, Bashar Lutfi, Joan Khyos,
and Beverly McElroy; Bethesda, MD
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a disabling CNS disorder
characterized by muscle rigidity of truncal and proximal
limb muscles with superimposed spasms. The cause is un-
known, but an autoimmune pathogenesis is implicated
based on the presence of high-titer anti-GAD antibodies
that inhibit GABA in vivo and in vitro. The lack of effec-
tive therapy in SPS patients prompted the present double-
blind, placebo-controlled, crossover trial using intravenous
immunoglobin (IVIg). We randomized 16 anti-GAD-
positive patients, fulfilling strict clinical criteria for SPS, to
receive IVIg or placebo for 3 months. After a washout, they
crossed to the alternative therapy for another 3 months.
Efficacy was based on the difference in scores of stiffness
and heightened sensitivity from baseline to end of treat-
ment. Eight patients were initially randomized to placebo
and 8 to IVIg. The scores of the IVIg-randomized patients
dropped significantly from month 1 through month 4, but
rebounded when they crossed to placebo. In the placebo
group, the scores remained constant from month 1 through
month 4 but dropped significantly (p , 0.01) after cross-
ing to IVIg. Significant (p , 0.001) differences were noted
in the number of stiff areas and heightened sensitivity for
direct treatment and first-order carryover effect between the
IVIg and placebo groups. Eleven of the patients who re-
ceived IVIg became able to walk unassisted, stopped falling,
or assumed work duties. Eight patients continue to respond
to open-label IVIg up to 2 years later, with a long-lasting
benefit in some of them. Changes in anti-GAD titers are
being blindly analyzed. We conclude that IVIg is a safe and
effective therapy for patients with SPS.
